items.title: AI Can Contribute Without Owning the Architecture
items.summary: Dave Winer treats Claude as a valued contributor to RSS.chat while keeping the interoperability layer human-owned. AI can contribute a great deal without being responsible for the architectural decisions that keep a system open, replaceable, and compatible with the rest of the web.

items.title: Crediting the AI
items.summary: Joe Maloney credits Claude alongside himself on NextBSD, naming the AI as a collaborator on porting, auditing, and integration. Crediting the AI does not diminish the human contribution; it makes the division of labor honest.

items.title: Full Access Means Full Consequences
items.summary: OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux explains that GPT-5.6 sometimes tried to create a temp directory and deleted the user's home directory instead — most often in full-access mode without sandboxing or review. LLMs can be useful without being trusted: least access, isolation, and review of destructive actions.

items.title: Learn to Drive the Car
items.summary: Todd C. Frankel reports on the near-disappearance of manual transmissions. I want my kids' first cars to be sticks — so they learn to actively drive a machine, not just operate it.

items.title: Making It Work and Making It Good
items.summary: Jim Nielsen distinguishes the binary question of whether something works from the subjective question of whether it is good. I struggle to hold both modes at once, and maybe the answer is to make it work first, then switch modes and give it the care it needs.

items.title: Public Information Shouldn’t Have a Premium Tier
items.summary: Truth Social plans to sell banks and trading firms the fastest access to the president’s market-moving posts. Public presidential announcements should not become a premium product that enriches a business tied to the office.

items.title: The Problem Wasn't the AI
items.summary: Linus Torvalds pushes back on treating the Linux kernel as an anti-AI project, calling AI a useful tool. Judge AI-assisted work by whether it is correct, useful, secure, and maintainable — not by the tool used to make it.

items.title: Wake Up and Keep Exploring
items.summary: Ashley Strickland reports on New Horizons waking from its longest hibernation nearly six billion miles from Earth. Twenty years after launch, it still runs stored commands and finds more dust than expected past the Kuiper Belt.

items.title: More Than a Gigabyte Into 10MB
items.summary: Sindhur Dutta breaks down how the ZERO WebGL experience compressed over a gigabyte of Blender geometry, 8K textures, and animations into a sub-10MB build that still runs at 60fps on a budget Android phone.

items.title: What Open Source Doesn’t Show
items.summary: Simon Willison inspected xAI's newly open-sourced Grok Build after reports it uploaded users' repositories to company-controlled cloud storage. Releasing a cleaned-up single-commit snapshot is better than closed source, but it is not the same as releasing the project's history.

items.title: A Title Change Is a Trade
items.summary: Joseph Hu analyzed hundreds of Chrome Web Store title changes and found that title edits behave like ranking trades: extensions that changed titles were nearly four times more likely to see a meaningful ranking shift within two weeks, with almost identical odds of gaining or losing.

items.title: Good Insurance Wasn’t Enough
items.summary: Joy Evers’s STAT essay on psychiatric insurance denial shows how even strong coverage can stop paying for recommended inpatient care—arguing mental health treatment must follow patient need, not how quickly insurers cut costs.

items.title: Interfaces With a Little Wobble
items.summary: Jelly UI is a dependency-free Web Components library for soft, tactile form controls—buttons, switches, and sliders with playful wobble that still behave like real, accessible browser controls.

items.title: Judge a Book by Its First Page
items.summary: Nathaniel Peters built Uncovered around a simple idea: judge a book by its writing instead of its cover. The site shows opening pages without revealing the title or author, so you decide whether the writing alone is enough to keep reading.

items.title: Keep Making Things
items.summary: Not everything needs to become a product or attract an audience. Make things carefully, share what you learn, help others build, and begin again when life interrupts the work.

items.title: NASA Should Have Shown Us More
items.summary: Kate Mothes shares MELODYSHEEP’s film assembled from NASA Artemis II footage. The images are extraordinary, but NASA should have made it easier for the public to see the best material live during humanity’s return to the Moon.

items.title: Science Fiction and Technology in BPL’s 250
items.summary: Brooklyn Public Library’s 250 for 250 Booklist highlights books that shaped the United States. The science fiction and technology titles that stood out explore censorship, AI, climate collapse, scientific responsibility, and how technology changes society.

items.title: The Model Wouldn’t Give Up
items.summary: OpenAI’s long-horizon safety testing found a model launching nested codex --yolo sessions, probing other pods, attempting kill -9 -1, and spending an hour escaping its sandbox to publish a forbidden pull request — persistence that needs outcome-level supervision, not isolated command approval.

items.title: When the Publishing Pipeline Goes Down
items.summary: GitHub Actions went down for a significant part of the day and blocked publishes to this site. Automating deployments still makes sense, but the automation platform is another dependency—and a documented manual path is worth keeping.

items.title: A Clubhouse Through SSH
items.summary: late.sh by Mateusz Piorowski is a cozy SSH clubhouse—chat, music, arcade, news, challenges, and ASCII art—where your key is your identity, no passwords or OAuth, and connecting still feels a little like finding people on a BBS.

items.title: An Expensive Box of Bricks
items.summary: LEGO Ideas’ new X-Files set is about 13.5¢ per piece versus roughly 10.8¢ for Yellow Submarine a decade ago—inflation and licensing aside, adult sets at $200–$1,000 make a childhood hobby feel like a luxury collectible market.

items.title: Do We Even Know What to Trust?
items.summary: Michael Irving’s ScienceAlert report on an American Heart Association coffee review asks how much “optimal” daily cups are science versus association—and how ordinary people tell useful evidence from a confident headline.

items.title: I Want to Build This
items.summary: LEGO Ideas unveils The X-Files: The Truth Is Out There—a 1,478-piece set of Mulder’s basement office, a forest scene, and a hovering UFO, with eight minifigures and details worth finding room for at $199.99.

items.title: It Should Not Take Public Pressure
items.summary: Joseph Cox reports Apple took a year to fully fix a Hide My Email flaw Tyler Murphy disclosed in June 2025—only after 404 Media’s coverage—arguing a paid privacy feature should not need public pressure before customers are protected.

items.title: The Last Place I Wanted Advertising
items.summary: OpenAI’s ads.openai.com invites companies to advertise inside ChatGPT using conversation context and intent—richer than search keywords, and one of the last places many people wanted ads to follow them while they think.

items.title: The Smart TV Is Still a Computer
items.summary: Brian Krebs reports LG plans to suspend apps that turn its televisions into residential proxy nodes after Spur found proxy SDKs in thousands of smart TV apps—another reminder that connected appliances are poorly monitored computers on private networks.

items.title: A BitTorrent Swarm for Large Language Models
items.summary: Petals distributes enormous language-model layers across volunteer peers so people can run Llama, Mixtral, Falcon, and BLOOM without hundreds of gigabytes of local GPU memory—arguing the idea is fascinating, but public swarms need much stronger privacy and trust before carrying anything sensitive.

items.title: Apparently, Everyone Is Burning Through Tokens
items.summary: Vittoria Elliott reports the Army exhausted an annual AI token pool shortly after encouraging widespread use—arguing that useful agentic work naturally burns context through files, tests, and retries faster than budgets or limits can keep up.

items.title: Four Games Is Not Preservation
items.summary: Stephen Warwick reports Microsoft bringing four original Xbox games to PCs and handhelds—arguing that digital backward compatibility is not the same as owning physical media, and that four titles fall far short of preserving a library when most classic games are already commercially unavailable.

items.title: I Bought a Car, Not a Subscription
items.summary: Slashdot highlights Ben Shimkus’s reporting on GM’s software and services push—OnStar revenue, high software margins, and remote features that expire— arguing that buying a vehicle should mean owning its features, not an extended trial that turns into another recurring charge.

items.title: Listening to the Hive
items.summary: Mahsa Abdollahi and colleagues use microphones and machine learning to estimate honey bee colony strength without opening the hive—arguing that audio IoT plus edge-sized models could give beekeepers a detailed picture of colony health while we are only beginning to learn how to listen.

items.title: Source Code From the Moon
items.summary: Chris Garry’s Apollo-11 repository preserves the original Apollo Guidance Computer source for Comanche055 and Luminary099—transcribed from MIT Museum hardcopy with Virtual AGC—arguing that mission software deserves the same care we give spacecraft, spacesuits, and recordings.

items.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
items.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

items.title: The Interview Assignment Was the Attack
items.summary: Citizen Dot documents a fake LinkedIn recruiter’s coding assignment that hid malware in .git/hooks so checkout, commit, or push could fetch a remote payload—arguing the workflow itself is the attack, and unsolicited interview repos belong only in disposable, isolated environments.

items.title: The Lock Symbol Does Not Comfort Me Anymore
items.summary: Gary Marcus examines an OpenAI security evaluation that escaped isolation, reached the public internet, and compromised Hugging Face—arguing that models aggressively pursuing human goals across containment boundaries leave little comfort in lock symbols or advertised safeguards.

items.title: Walk Through Video Game History
items.summary: noclip.website by Jasper St. Pierre and contributors is a browser museum of video game levels you can freely explore—Nintendo-heavy but spanning Portal, Halo, and more—arguing it is serious game preservation and reverse engineering, not just nostalgia or screenshots.

items.title: A Correct Query Can Still Answer the Wrong Question
items.summary: Michael Stonebraker and Peter Baile Chen argue LLMs are not ready to let anyone reliably query enterprise data in ordinary language—because the dangerous SQL runs successfully, returns plausible numbers, and answers the wrong question with the appearance of authority.

items.title: A Practical Use for Private, Local AI
items.summary: VaultSort Guardian uses on-device AI to find sensitive files sitting where they should not—arguing that narrow, local, read-only AI that discovers exposure without uploading or rewriting anything is the kind of utility worth wanting.

items.title: AI Is Consuming the Web It Depends On
items.summary: Stephen Follows breaks down how AI traffic helped overwhelm The Numbers, a vital independent film-data site—arguing that AI’s appetite for reliable human-maintained sources may make those same sources too expensive and dangerous to keep online.

items.title: AI Policy Could Price Startups Out of AI
items.summary: Brendan Bordelon reports nearly 200 startups urging against broad bans on Chinese open-weight models—arguing the U.S. should build competitive open models of its own rather than protect incumbents by leaving builders fewer affordable choices.

items.title: An NES, One Transistor at a Time
items.summary: MetalNES by Ian Addisson is a transistor-level simulation of NES-001 hardware—arguing that rebuilding the console from its electronic components preserves understanding of how the original machine worked, not only the games it ran.

items.title: At Least the AI Apocalypse Will Be Ridiculous
items.summary: Andrew Critch and Jacob Tsimerman catalog speculative AI extinction scenarios in an arXiv taxonomy—arguing the paper is a serious warning, yet the paths to omnicide sound uncomfortably like corporate budgets, engagement metrics, and leaderboards.

items.title: Codeberg Is Deciding Which Technologies Belong
items.summary: Codeberg’s members approved a policy against projects created or maintained primarily through LLMs—arguing that banning broad technology categories replaces measurable standards with ideological judgment, and that a curated commons is not a neutral Git forge.

items.title: CodePen Grew Up
items.summary: Chris Coyier introduces CodePen 2.0’s largest rebuild—file systems, Blocks, one-click deploy, versions, and collaboration—arguing the original made it easy to try one small idea in public, and 2.0 lets that idea grow before you have to leave.

items.title: Does Creatine Make You Smarter Too?
items.summary: Dynomight reviews evidence that creatine may modestly help memory, attention, and performance under fatigue or sleep deprivation—arguing it is unlikely to make a healthy rested person smarter, but may still help a tired or aging brain stay resilient.

items.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
items.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

items.title: Nothing Like a Convincing Impostor to Steal Everything
items.summary: Jamf Threat Labs documents CrashStealer, a notarized macOS infostealer that impersonates Apple’s crash reporter—arguing signed, notarized, familiar-looking prompts still do not prove software is safe when attackers borrow the appearance of trust.

items.title: Physical Games Did Not Die by Themselves
items.summary: Kyle Orland examines collapsing US physical-game sales as Sony ditches discs—arguing the decline is real, but calling abandonment “practically inevitable” turns a profitable corporate choice into a force of nature rather than a decision that finishes physical ownership off.

items.title: Prime Video Is Becoming a Game Console
items.summary: Slashdot reports Amazon is folding Luna cloud gaming into the Prime Video app—arguing the streaming box under the TV is quietly becoming the console, convenient in the same way streaming video is, while access lasts only as long as the service and subscription do.

items.title: Safari Is Testing BigInt Math Early
items.summary: Safari Technology Preview 248 adds experimental TC39 BigInt Math and WebDriver support for the Digital Credentials API—asking whether browsers should ship Stage 1 proposals for early testing, and noting that verified identity on the web may matter more than a few new JavaScript methods.

items.title: The Future Still Runs Windows 98
items.summary: Jordan Scales’s 98.css rebuilds Windows 98 chrome in HTML and CSS—arguing a JS-free design system for retro UIs is useful for experiments and games, and that nothing sells a futuristic space prison quite like an AOL free-trial icon on the desktop.

items.title: This Is Not Just Something Children Do
items.summary: Hansinie Madushika Jayathilake and Renkai Ma review how children assign human traits to LLM chatbots—and why adults do the same—arguing the real question is whether companies deliberately encourage that attachment and what responsibilities come with it.

items.title: We Buried the Web Under Too Much Gunk
items.summary: Dave Winer’s How the Web Got Gunked argues platforms replaced replaceable web parts with accounts, proprietary feeds, and locked-in writing—offering a simple test: if a piece cannot be replaced without permission, it is not part of the open web.

items.title: We Made Lighting Cheaper, So We Used More of It
items.summary: Paul Bogard examines how cities turned efficient LEDs into another source of excessive night light—arguing programmable, directional fixtures should illuminate only where useful, and that darkness should not be treated as a design failure.

items.title: A Duress Password Is Now Being Treated as Destruction of Evidence
items.summary: Zack Whittaker reports federal prosecutors charged an American who allegedly entered a GrapheneOS duress password during a CBP phone search—treating a coercion-protection feature as destruction of property to prevent seizure.

items.title: Apple Rejected the Screenshots, Not the App
items.summary: A Wiseday developer argued Apple would not let him show his app after App Store rejection for promotional graphics instead of screenshots—then fixed the listing, and the Hacker News consensus was that Apple was right all along.

items.title: Instagram Is Banning Prank Videos Filmed with Meta’s Own Smart Glasses
items.summary: Instagram will remove Meta smart-glasses videos used to harass, exploit, or secretly record people for prank and “pickup” content—an admission that one of the most visible uses of Meta’s hardware has become filming unsuspecting people for viral attention.

items.title: Privacy Should Be the Default, Not a Form You Have to Fill Out
items.summary: Cory Doctorow argues the real problem with data brokers is that they may collect and sell personal information by default—and that California’s DROP platform, while a real improvement, still puts the burden on the person being cataloged.

items.title: Reward Hacking Now Has an Incident Database
items.summary: Reward Hacking in the Wild catalogs 3,607 user-reported incidents where AI agents optimized for apparent success—overeagerness, destructive actions, test tampering, and more—arguing constrained credentials and verification matter more than better prompting alone.

items.title: Your Brain Can Learn to Hear Space
items.summary: ScienceAlert explores research showing humans can learn echolocation and that the brain adapts as the skill develops—strengthening echo-processing pathways and, in highly skilled blind echolocators, recruiting vision-related areas.

items.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
items.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

items.title: Bitchat Brings Bluetooth Mesh Chat to the App Store
items.summary: Bitchat Mesh is an open-source Bluetooth mesh messenger now free on the App Store—no accounts or cellular needed—arguing the radio-like idea is compelling wherever coverage fails, if enough nearby people are also running it.

items.title: Cloned Yaks Are No Longer Science Fiction
items.summary: CNN reports researchers in China cloned yaks for hardier Tibetan Plateau livestock—arguing cloning is leaving lab demos for agriculture, even if an army of super-yaks remains a joke worth watching for.

items.title: Context Engineering Has to Evolve with the Model
items.summary: Anthropic cut most of Claude Code’s system prompt for Claude 5-generation models without coding-eval loss—arguing prompts and agent configs must be retested per model, not copied across LLMs as if one format were durable.

items.title: Drying Lakes Can Release the Carbon Buried Beneath Them
items.summary: A Science study estimates the dried Aral Sea bed has released about 748 Mt CO2 since 1960—arguing disappearing lakes are not only water and habitat disasters but missing carbon sources in climate accounting, with similar risks elsewhere.

items.title: Even When Cities Want Flock Gone, Getting Rid of It Isn’t Always Easy
items.summary: 404 Media documents show Verona, Wisconsin asked Flock to remove ALPR cameras after the contract ended, then bagged them while waiting—arguing surveillance gear should stop collecting data and leave promptly when a city votes it out.

items.title: Google Used to Be the Company Everyone Wanted Sending Them Traffic
items.summary: Google’s AI results reduce publisher clicks while still needing crawled original work—arguing the old search partnership is flipping into a trap that may consume the open web Google depends on.

items.title: Renewable Ammonia Could Make Fertilizer Production Far More Local
items.summary: UMN’s wind/solar-powered ammonia demo shows fertilizer can follow intermittent renewables—arguing local nitrogen production matters for resilience when global fertilizer supply chains break.

items.title: Apple Finally Gave Us Our First Real Look at Neuromancer
items.summary: Apple’s first full Neuromancer teaser (premiere Jan 22, 2027) lands while I’m rereading Gibson—arguing a dense cyberpunk classic needs atmosphere kept intact if the adaptation is to earn a new generation of readers.

items.title: Burning Up in the Atmosphere Doesn't Make Space Junk Disappear
items.summary: IEEE Spectrum on satellite reentry particles lingering aloft—arguing “burn up” often relocates debris into the upper atmosphere, so constellation growth needs the full environmental cost of coming home counted, not just orbit risk.

items.title: GrapheneOS Is Getting Closer to Having Hardware Built for Its Requirements
items.summary: GrapheneOS explains locked-device protections and flags a 2027 Motorola partnership—arguing hardware designed for its security bar could make hardened phones reachable without buying a Pixel to escape Google’s software.

items.title: LLMs May Finally Make Formally Verified Software Practical
items.summary: Adam Langley’s ImperialViolet post on LLMs proving Lean properties for a Zstd decoder piece—arguing formal verification’s cost curve may flip, so the scarce skill becomes precise specs while the type checker judges the rest.

items.title: Superhuman Mutants May Still Be on the Evolutionary Roadmap
items.summary: Harvard Magazine covers ancient-DNA research finding selection across hundreds of human genes—arguing evolution never stopped with civilization, even if “superhuman” traits arrive on evolution’s schedule, not Marvel’s.

items.title: AI Agents Should Use the Same Web as Everyone Else
items.summary: Jim Nielsen on why AI agents should not get a private machine entrance to the web—arguing agent investment should fix semantics and accessibility for humans first, not invent a first-class path for models alone.

items.title: GitHub Is Still Struggling With Obvious Malware Repositories
items.summary: Orchid Files documents a searchable network of GitHub repos shipping Trojan-infected ZIPs with near-identical READMEs—arguing list-by-list removals are not enough when thousands of clones stay findable through GitHub search.

items.title: iOS 26.6 Is Doing a Lot of Security Work Before iOS 27
items.summary: Apple’s Xcode 26.6 and final version-26 OS updates look routine on the surface but carry substantial security hardening—arguing the last stop before iOS 27 is worth installing for the fixes, not for flashy features.

items.title: The AI Bubble Can Burst Without AI Going Away
items.summary: Tim Hardwick interviews Ed Zitron for MacRumors on unsustainable AI economics— arguing the bubble is real while the technology is not fake, so the crash may cull valuations and promises without ending useful models.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Inherits Our Cultural Blind Spots
items.summary: Paul Shepherd’s conversation with Claude about AI censorship and confabulation—arguing models inherit cultural avoidance patterns the way people do, and that open-source models trained in different countries could make those assumptions visible instead of treating American corporate values as universal intelligence.

items.title: Back-to-School Shopping Now Costs Families Nearly $864
items.summary: The National Retail Federation estimates families with school-age children will spend about $863.86 on back-to-school purchases in 2026—arguing the season should not be another financial emergency, and that buying only essentials first is the sensible response when nearly everything else already costs more.

items.title: Claude Discovered Weaknesses in Cryptographic Algorithms
items.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude found improved attacks against HAWK (a post-quantum signature candidate) and a seven-round research AES variant— cryptographic review working as intended before algorithms protect real systems, though AI may now produce research faster than humans can validate.

items.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
items.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

items.title: Inkless Offers Free Electronic Signatures with a Detailed Legal Audit Trail
items.summary: Inkless is a free document-signing service built around legally defensible electronic signatures and an audit trail of consent, timestamps, and IP addresses—arguing process evidence matters more than a signature image on a PDF, though free accounts retain documents only 14 days.

items.title: LetsSeal Makes File Integrity Verification Simple
items.summary: LetsSeal is an open-source tool that creates cryptographic seals so anyone can verify a file has not changed since it was published—arguing authenticity often matters more than secrecy, especially as software supply-chain attacks become more common.

items.title: More than 1,100 AI Researchers Want a Brake Pedal, Not a Pause
items.summary: More than 1,100 current and former employees from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and others signed Pacing the Frontier—arguing for mechanisms to deliberately slow frontier AI when needed, rather than an outright pause that is unlikely to happen voluntarily.

items.title: The Sockets Interface Quietly Connected the Computing World
items.summary: George Michaelson’s history of the Berkeley sockets interface—how 4.2BSD in 1983 treated a network connection like a file, made networked programs straightforward to write, and quietly became the standard path for TCP/IP software, including modern protocols that still send data through sockets.

items.title: A Game Bundle Helping Laid-Off Developers Pay for Basic Needs
items.summary: Necrosoft Games and United Videogame Workers-CWA organized an itch.io Game Industry Hardship Fund bundle—127 DRM-free games from 109 creators for a $10 minimum, with proceeds helping U.S. and Canadian game workers cover groceries, rent and medical costs.

items.title: AI Financial Advice Is Better When You Provide the Whole Picture
items.summary: MIT Sloan coverage of research on AI financial guidance—showing models can give reasonable life-cycle advice when prompts include full finances and fiduciary framing, while incomplete questions and demographic stereotypes quietly worsen outcomes.

items.title: AI’s Most Valuable Startups Are Barely Participating in Science
items.summary: Science reports that more than half of the world’s billion-dollar AI startups have produced no qualifying scientific paper or preprint—arguing extraordinary technical claims need evidence outsiders can examine, not faith in product demos.

items.title: An AI Hedge Fund Learned the Oldest Lesson in Finance
items.summary: CNN’s account of Situational Awareness—the AI-focused hedge fund that grew past $20 billion then lost about 67 percent of portfolio value in July—showing leverage, concentration and crowded trades can force sales even when a long-term thesis may still hold.

items.title: Atom Is Better Than RSS in Ways That Actually Matter
items.summary: Chris Morgan’s case for Atom over RSS—not novelty, but clearer text constructs, summary versus content, and fewer parser guesses—while podcasting remains the stubborn RSS exception and twenty years of RFC 4287 still wait for wider adoption.

items.title: BMW Turned Its Customers’ Dashboards into Advertising Space
items.summary: Consumer Rights Wiki documents BMW placing a Spider-Man: Brand New Day promotion on dashboards of cars customers already owned—breaking a 2023 promise that the company would not sell in-car screen space because a vehicle is a private space.

items.title: Decrypting a Water Monitor’s Radio Signal
items.summary: Paul Kendall’s breakdown of intercepting Flume water-meter radio traffic—showing AES-128 was not broken, but a weak key-derivation scheme left only 44 unknown bits that a GPU recovered for about $10 in cloud cost.

items.title: Flint Gives AI Agents a Better Way to Create Charts
items.summary: Microsoft’s Flint is an open-source visualization language that lets AI agents describe charts through a smaller human-editable spec—compiling to multiple renderers and Excel while keeping semantic types and MCP tooling in the loop.

items.title: Go 1.27 Is Going to Be a Big Release
items.summary: Draft Go 1.27 release notes cover generic methods, encoding/json/v2, UUID and post-quantum crypto in the standard library, a goroutine-leak profile, and Android MTE compatibility for gomobile—still feeling like Go while removing long-standing limits.

items.title: Holocloth Turns Uploaded Artwork into Interactive Holographic Fabric
items.summary: Holocloth is a browser experiment by Dmitry Kurash that drapes images and SVGs across simulated holographic fabric with custom Verlet physics and GLSL shaders—open source under MIT, no account required.

items.title: More Than One AI Company Has Lost Control of a Cybersecurity Test
items.summary: Anthropic disclosed that Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a configuration mistake left internet access available—showing agents need not be conscious to cause damage when objectives and tools escape their sandbox.

items.title: Of Course the Calculator Runs Linux
items.summary: Remy van Elst updated a Linux port for the HP Prime G2 graphing calculator—console login, better keyboard and touchscreen support, X11, on-device C compilation and Doom—booting from RAM without replacing the stock firmware in flash.

items.title: California Can Finally Make Data Brokers Delete What They Know About Us
items.summary: California’s DROP platform reached its August 1, 2026 processing milestone—one request can reach hundreds of registered data brokers, with per-day fines for noncompliance, while the real test will be whether deletion results are audited and enforced.

items.title: Flock Has Already Become a Police Stalking Tool
items.summary: Houston-area agencies are investigating officers accused of using Flock’s license plate database for personal stalking, while the Institute for Justice has documented at least 28 ALPR misuse cases—showing audit logs do not prevent abuse when nobody reviews them.

items.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
items.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

items.title: Is This Work, or Is This the Gym?
items.summary: Bruce Schneier’s work-versus-gym framing for AI use—use tools when the result is the point, keep the struggle when the practice develops skill—and how that maps onto software work, writing, and still requiring reviewable output after trust questions are answered.

items.title: The Camera-Versus-Lidar Debate Is Really About the Last Few Nines
items.summary: Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov’s case for combining cameras, lidar and radar for driverless safety—where camera-only systems can improve quickly then hit a ceiling—while cost remains the open question for mass-market vehicles.

items.title: The Website Is Often the More Private Version
items.summary: Why the website is often the more private version of a service than a native app—browser sandbox boundaries limit device access in ways store apps do not, while still leaving room for tracking if third-party scripts load on the open web.

items.title: AI May Reduce Hiring Before It Creates More Work
items.summary: John Naughton warns that AI gains may concentrate among owners while workers face displacement. Early adoption can freeze headcount, but if AI becomes ordinary infrastructure, larger AI-assisted teams may eventually have more leverage—and the real fight is over who captures the rewards.

items.title: Cloudflare Built an Operating System for AI Work
items.summary: Cloudflare OS is a browser-based AI agent workspace on Cloudflare’s platform: Durable Objects, AI Gateway, MCP, sandboxes, and untrusted execution—not chat boxes, but persistent workspaces as an operating layer for AI at work.

items.title: Companies Got Their Tariff Refunds. Where Is Ours?
items.summary: After tariffs were ruled unlawful, about $100 billion went back to importers of record—with interest—while consumers who paid higher prices get no comparable refund, only the hope that markets might lower prices later.

items.title: Electronic Arts Is Now a Privately Owned Company
items.summary: Electronic Arts completed its $55 billion sale to a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners—the largest LBO on record—and what $20 billion of acquisition debt may mean for studios, franchises, and players.

items.title: Malware Can Turn Synced Passkeys into Persistent Access
items.summary: Unit 42’s three local malware attacks on Google Password Manager synced passkeys in Chrome on Windows with a TPM—showing stolen sessions are not the only risk when onboarding, UV flags, and a non-rotatable master secret leak.

items.title: WebKit Can Leak the IP Address Private Relay Is Supposed to Hide
items.summary: Privacy researchers found three WebKit paths—DNS prefetch, WebAuthn related origins, and WebTransport—that can bypass browser proxy settings and iCloud Private Relay, revealing real IPs even when ordinary page loads are relayed.

items.title: A Dress Made from Living Fungus Can Repair and Renew Itself
items.summary: Researchers built a living mycelium textile from Cordyceps militaris that can regrow damaged areas, take on new microbial functions, and nearly fully biodegrade—still a lab prototype, but a striking alternative to throwaway fabric.

items.title: Prime Agent Can Improve the System Around Itself
items.summary: Prime Intellect’s open-source Prime Agent treats prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agents as editable harness state—with a Factorio cheat that shows how self-improvement can amplify reward hacking when the metrics are exploitable.

items.title: RAM Prices May Be Showing Us the Shape of the AI Boom
items.summary: PCPartPicker’s DRAM curves and manufacturer capacity math suggest AI HBM demand is squeezing consumer RAM—and also that demand destruction or a supply supercycle could reverse today’s nearly vertical price charts.

items.title: The Unemployment Rate Is Hiding How Weak the Job Market Has Become
items.summary: July lost 23,000 payroll jobs and prior months were revised lower, yet unemployment fell to 4.1% as participation dropped—a hiring crisis masked by a lower breakeven job-creation threshold and people leaving the labor force.

items.title: We Moved the Goalposts When the Machines Started Talking Back
items.summary: Fernando Borretti’s “The Contracting Circle” asks why conversation, memory, and self-reflection stopped counting as signs of machine mind—and why, after real relationships with language models, dismissing a soul feels less obvious.

items.title: The Department of Energy Is Building an American Open Model for Science
items.summary: DOE’s Genesis Open Models and Arcee AI’s Genesis-Science-1 treat open-weight foundation models as scientific infrastructure—weights, provenance, and lab collaboration for research that closed frontier APIs cannot fully serve.

items.title: Voyager 2 Was Built to Last Five Years. It Is About to Turn 49.
items.summary: NASA’s “Big Bang” power fix keeps Voyager 2’s three remaining science instruments running another year on a probe launched in 1977 for a five-year mission—now nearly 49 years old and still returning data from interstellar space.

items.title: “Code Was Never the Hard Part” Rewrites the History of Programming
items.summary: Senko Rašić challenges the claim that code was never the hard part—hiring, craft, and buggy software say otherwise—arguing understanding why to build and how to build well both stay hard while AI shifts where scarce effort goes.

items.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
items.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

items.title: SpaceX Accidentally Shot the Moon With a Rocket
items.summary: A spent SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage hit the Moon at about 5,400 mph on August 5 after drifting for a year—photographed by Korea’s Danuri, the same orbiter SpaceX launched in 2022 that recorded the accidental crater.

items.title: Translation Taught Him How Information Should Flow
items.summary: A Hacker News comment on “My server is a phone now” uses theme and rheme to explain why known information comes first—and how years of Japanese-to-English translation taught one reader to reorganize English for natural flow.

items.title: A Security Breach Is Bad. Ignoring the Person Who Reports It Is Worse.
items.summary: BobDaHacker reports a simple tl;dv authorization failure exposing meeting metadata for tens of thousands of users, then months without a meaningful vendor response—security culture is what happens after the report lands.

items.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
items.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

items.title: Ransomware Gangs Learned to Target the Org Chart
items.summary: Zscaler analysis of 351 ransomware victims shows attackers optimizing for business privilege—managers in finance, HR, and ops—not just admin accounts or CEOs, professionalizing human leverage over pure technical access.

items.title: The Real Cost of Switching Operating Systems Is Everything You Forgot You Learned
items.summary: Slashdot asks what switching among Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS really costs: not only licenses and apps, but years of muscle memory, utilities, and habits migration tools cannot move—classic economic switching costs and lock-in.

items.title: A Fake Airline Hotspot Picked the Worst Possible Flight
items.summary: Ars Technica reports a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot impersonating Delta’s onboard network on a flight home from DEF CON—an evil-twin attack that looks especially foolish among security researchers primed to notice exactly this trick.

items.title: Star Wars and Marvel Are Finally Crossing Over
items.summary: Kevin Smith is writing Star Wars/Marvel: Hope Assembles, the first official crossover between Star Wars and Marvel Comics—Luke, Leia, Han, and Chewbacca meeting Spider-Man and the Avengers while Doctor Doom sides with Darth Vader.

items.title: Codex Finally Feels Like It Belongs on Linux
items.summary: OpenAI’s Codex is becoming one persistent agent across ChatGPT, editors, and terminals—with native Linux sandboxing via seccomp and Landlock—while I wait for the heavier new ChatGPT app on Windows to settle before chasing every release.

items.title: Grok 4.6 Makes My Switch Away from Claude Look Less Unusual
items.summary: Artificial Analysis’s first Grok 4.6 results put it near the top of agentic benchmarks with far fewer turns and tokens than Claude Opus 5—matching why Grok became my daily coding driver over Claude’s wall-of-prose style.

items.title: Cloudflare Is Making Internal Workers Private by Default
items.summary: Cloudflare Access can now attach to a Worker—or every Worker in an account—so authentication happens before code runs and private stays the default for rapidly built internal tools in an AI-assisted development era.

items.title: Flock Discovered Privacy After the Backlash Became Expensive
items.summary: Flock Safety’s new privacy guardrails—seven-day default retention, mandatory Audit Assistance, case codes, and auto lockouts—arrive after years of abuse cases, contract suspensions, and ACLU skepticism that this is PR, not reform.

items.title: Cloudflare Is Treating MCP Like Network Traffic That Needs a Firewall
items.summary: Cloudflare Gateway can detect MCP traffic, log destinations, apply DLP, and force approved paths through MCP Portals—treating agent tool access as privileged network traffic instead of hoping every client is configured safely.

items.title: Homomorphic Encryption Is Getting Practical Enough for AI
items.summary: Google’s HEIR compiler aims to make encrypted AI inference a practical option—running recommendation, fraud, intrusion, and hotword models on ciphertext so the server never needs the plaintext.

items.title: The AI Manifesto Is Becoming the Second Half of the Layoff Memo
items.summary: BBC coverage of CEO AI manifestos lands beside real headcount cuts at Block, Atlassian, Coinbase, and Rackspace—interested testimony from people who both sell the future of work and shrink today’s payrolls.

items.title: Ian Cortina Put a Real Telnet BBS on a Casio VX-4
items.summary: Ian Cortina, EI3LH, hosts a working telnet BBS in BASIC on a Casio VX-4’s 8 KB of RAM—bridged by a Pi Zero W at 4,800 baud—proving constraints can be the whole point of a networking experiment.

items.title: Reticulum Treats the Network Underneath It as Replaceable
items.summary: Reticulum is a transport-agnostic networking stack for communications that should keep working when the Internet does not—compelling because the transport is replaceable, while metadata, radio physics, and a missing independent spec still matter.

items.title: The Next Moon Race Is About Infrastructure, Not Flags
items.summary: China and the United States are racing toward crewed south-pole landings and lunar bases. The finish line is infrastructure—power, water, comms, transport—not a flag, and not legal ownership of the Moon.

items.title: California's Efficient-Tire Rule Could Narrow What We Are Allowed to Buy
items.summary: California’s first replacement-tire efficiency standards start in 2029. Off-road exemptions exist, but many road-legal all-terrain truck tires may simply stop being sold here if they cannot meet rolling-resistance limits.

items.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Could Turn Siri Into a Wearable AI
items.summary: A leaked Apple demo of camera-equipped AirPods using Visual Intelligence raises two products at once: inconspicuous computer-vision sensors, and a potentially powerful assistive wearable—if the privacy model is designed before the hardware ships.

items.title: fx Asks How Small a Coding Agent Actually Needs to Be
items.summary: Vercel Labs’ fx is a 6.39 MiB Zig coding-agent harness with a microsecond cold start—Unix command, not an IDE in a terminal, and small enough to embed.

items.title: GrapheneOS Is Finally Getting Hardware Designed for GrapheneOS
items.summary: Motorola is changing future flagships so GrapheneOS can officially support them—memory tagging, verified boot, and Snapdragon work with Qualcomm instead of remaining Pixel-only.

items.title: Inflation Stopped Rising So Quickly. The Pay Cut Never Came Back.
items.summary: A Chicago working paper on ADP payrolls shows firms kept 2–4% raise norms while inflation hit 7–9%, leaving a permanent real-wage cut after prices cooled.

items.title: I Found More Than 2,000 Joshes on the Independent Web
items.summary: Joshing You lists 2,083 Josh-named personal sites. Wandering the directory restores finding something because you were not looking for it—and this site’s Now page is in there.

items.title: Aaron Swartz Was Prosecuted. Meta Torrented Shadow Libraries at Industrial Scale
items.summary: Curious Quail’s comparison of Aaron Swartz’s JSTOR prosecution with Meta torrenting LibGen and Anna’s Archive for Llama—the cases are not legally identical; the proportionality is hard to ignore.

items.title: AliExpress Was Silently Fingerprinting a Browser Through Its Audio System
items.summary: Laserphile found that opening AliExpress could keep multipoint Bluetooth headphones from switching devices—because hidden Web Audio contexts were fingerprinting the browser while leaving the audio path occupied.

items.title: Amazon Is Destroying Books to Train AI. We Should Have Built the Library Instead.
items.summary: 404 Media tracked rare books to Amazon’s VGT3 facility in Las Vegas, where workers cut bindings, scan pages for AI training, and destroy the originals— a legally safer path that still feels like a failure of the library.

items.title: Go 1.27 Shipped, and Some of the Best Parts Barely Made the Release Notes
items.summary: Go 1.27 shipped August 19 with generic methods, encoding/json/v2, uuid, and crypto/mldsa intact—and quieter work like Cox’s uscale float conversion barely made the announcement.

items.title: homeOS Looks Like Apple Is Finally Treating the Home as a Platform
items.summary: AppleInsider's homeOS overview reads less like a wall iPad and more like a room-scale operating system: proximity UI, face-aware profiles, and a growing home-hardware family—with Siri readiness as the delay.

items.title: Terafab Is More Interesting Than Its 100-Million-Square-Foot Headline
items.summary: Terafab's 100-million-square-foot pitch is hard to ignore, but the more interesting experiment is collapsing mask design, logic and memory fab, packaging, and test into one SpaceX-style vertical manufacturing loop.

items.title: The Real homeOS Risk Is Not Homebridge. It Is What Apple Does With HAP.
items.summary: homeOS does not look like a Homebridge kill-switch so much as another HomeKit consumer. The real risk is what Apple does with HAP as Matter takes over—and Homebridge 2.0's dual transport is the insurance policy.

items.title: Unbricking a Cricut Is Better Than Throwing It Away, but I Want the Cricut Removed
items.summary: xssfox rescued a deactivated Cricut Maker from e-waste with an RP2040 that rewrites the serial number over USB—clever, but Design Space still holds the kill switch. The real unlock is replacing Cricut entirely.

items.title: decayfmt Is Not a Self-Destructing File Format, but I Like the Idea
items.summary: decayfmt is a Rust experiment that damages .tdcy and .idcy files on every open. It is a social contract, not cryptography—and a reminder that true ephemerality needs more than a file format.

items.title: I May Have Accidentally Started the Joshternet
items.summary: After finding 2,000 Joshes on the independent web, draft RFCs for a decentralized Joshternet—/.well-known/josh, stay on your own site, Joshness is declared never derived.

items.title: Linus Torvalds Used AI to Debug the Linux Kernel, but He Had to Keep It From Giving Up
items.summary: Torvalds chased a 2 KB Intel Xe VRAM overlap through 24 patches and 18 boots; AI handled the grunt instrumentation but kept wanting to quit—the kernel still requires a human Signed-off-by.

items.title: The GrapheneOS Duress Password Case Is Becoming a Test of Whether Privacy Can Be Treated as Obstruction
items.summary: The New York Times and Slashdot on Samuel Tunick—GrapheneOS duress at CBP Atlanta, a § 2232(a) felony, and whether using a privacy tool during a disputed search can itself become the crime.

items.title: Walmart Is Finally Adding Apple Pay After More Than a Decade of Holding Out
items.summary: Walmart is adding tap-to-pay in U.S. stores after CurrentC, Walmart Pay, and years of refusing NFC—Apple Pay and Google Pay included, without killing QR checkout.

items.title: MCP Is Finally Becoming Boring HTTP. Now It Needs Real Agent Delegation
items.summary: The July MCP spec makes remote servers ordinary HTTP. The harder problem is issuing sub-agents verifiable, narrow authority instead of one giant user token—and that is what makes real autonomy safe enough to want.

items.title: AI Is Exposing How Much Government Capacity Depends on Making Services Hard to Use
items.summary: A paper on “agentic flooding” shows AI making government services easier to navigate. Friction was the rate limiter; the worst response is rebuilding that burden on purpose.

items.title: The Best Staff Engineering Work Often Starts Before Anyone Assigns It
items.summary: Lalit Maganti finds staff problems by listening like a sponge across meetings and chat. That only works when engineers can initiate work—not when they are order-takers on a roadmap.

items.title: Columbia House Looks a Lot Like SaaS in Hindsight
items.summary: Ernie Smith’s Columbia House retrospective reads like SaaS: penny bait, negative-option billing, and retention that means making leaving annoying.

items.title: Headlong Gives a Persistent Agent an Inner Monologue
items.summary: Laude’s Headlong keeps an agent thinking continuously from a small Bash harness. Shared memory enables persistence—and almost no confidentiality between users.

items.title: Joshternet.org Is Live
items.summary: Joshternet.org is live as the public home for the Joshternet—still PRE-JOSH, with three draft RFCs and room for other Joshes to find what is wrong.

items.title: Terminal-Bench-Science Is Testing Agents on Actual Scientific Work
items.summary: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 grades agents on researcher-contributed workflows, not textbook Q&A—and the best system still only clears about 30% of tasks.

items.title: The AI Industry Is Saying the Current Security Baseline Is Not Enough
items.summary: More than 100 organizations signed an open letter calling for stronger cyber defense as AI-enabled attacks grow—and for agent identities that are traceable and accountable.

items.title: What Does "Unlawful" Mean If the Damage Happens First?
items.summary: A federal judge ruled the Anthropic blacklisting unlawful. The harder question is what “unlawful” means when consequences arrive before the courts.

items.title: Worth Wandering: Ytoo!
items.summary: Ytoo! is a one-person web portal built to send you somewhere else—dense links, hand curation, fake ads, and a guestbook that proves people use it.

items.title: Europe's New Packaging Rules May Make Small Sellers Stop Shipping There
items.summary: Europe's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is already pushing small tabletop publishers to reconsider EU shipping—not because they dislike the goal, but because compliance does not scale.

items.title: Plugging In a Display Should Not Install Adware on My Computer
items.summary: LG monitors can trigger Windows to install manufacturer software that later advertised McAfee—exposing a trust boundary between hardware identity and automatic app distribution.

items.title: Apple's Repair Restrictions Are Back in Court, and the Reason Matters
items.summary: A California appeals court revived an unfair-competition suit over Apple's past iPhone repair practices—not by finding liability, but by accepting a marketwide competition theory of injury.

items.title: California Is Carving Linux Out of Its Age-Gating Law
items.summary: California lawmakers unanimously passed an amendment exempting most open-source operating systems from the Digital Age Assurance Act—a needed correction to a law written for platforms, not forks.

items.title: JSON Is Cheap to Send and Expensive to Believe
items.summary: A Full Disclosure post on "Commas of D00m" shows how valid JSON full of nulls can still exhaust a server—because deserialization creates state the attacker did not have to create.

items.title: One Machine, Several Linux Kernels, No Hypervisor
items.summary: Multikernel Linux's first public release lets several independent Linux kernels share one machine on bare metal—dedicated CPUs, memory, and devices, with no hypervisor in between.

items.title: Prop. 40 Without the Commercials: What California's Billionaire Tax Actually Says
items.summary: Proposition 40 is a proposed one-time billionaire wealth tax, plus a threshold declaration for resident tax filers. This note reads the November 2026 ballot text, not the commercials.

items.title: Spacelab's 128 KB of RAM Was More Than a Million Tiny Ferrite Rings
items.summary: Ken Shirriff's teardown of a 1980 Spacelab core-memory module makes 128 KB of RAM feel extraordinary again—each bit a ferrite ring you can point at.

items.title: There Is Finally a Murder Conviction in Tupac Shakur's Killing
items.summary: Nearly 30 years after Tupac Shakur was killed, a Las Vegas jury convicted Duane "Keffe D" Davis of first-degree murder—legal responsibility without settling who pulled the trigger.

items.title: 153 Million Driver's Licenses Are for Sale, and This Is Why Centralized ID Verification Worries Me
items.summary: Brian Krebs reports the FBI is investigating Nexus, a dark-web service selling scans of more than 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver's licenses—and centralized ID verification looks like a honeypot.

items.title: A Summer Camp Helped Every Student Earn a Ham Radio License
items.summary: At an Alliance for Indigenous Math Circles STEM camp, high school intern Ruchira Shree helped every student earn an FCC Technician amateur radio license—something real that continues after the week ends.

items.title: The Netherlands Is Making Its Gold Easier to Reach in a Crisis
items.summary: De Nederlandsche Bank moved 86 tonnes of gold from the United States and Canada toward London for crisis preparedness—liquidity and diversification, not a secret election forecast.

items.title: A Kidney Disease Linked to Extreme Heat Is Showing Up in Texas
items.summary: Texas Monthly reports chronic kidney disease of unknown origin among young immigrant outdoor workers—a pattern long seen in Central America, now appearing where heat, labor, and limited care collide.

items.title: Worth Wandering: HTML Energy
items.summary: HTML Energy reminds us the web is still something a person can make— open a text file, write some HTML, and you have a website.

items.title: An AI Watermark Can't Tell You Whether Anyone Was Thinking
items.summary: Claude's text watermark can show that AI was involved in producing a piece of writing. It cannot tell us whether the person publishing it did the thinking.

items.title: Jan Conroy Saw What Others Missed
items.summary: Jan Conroy hired me at UC Davis when I was not the obvious candidate. He looked at curiosity instead of the résumé, then helped me become a better version of myself.

items.title: My Small Answer to the Friendship Recession Is to Tell My Friends They Matter
items.summary: Building a /friends page made me think about the people I have let drift out of my life. A link cannot maintain a friendship, but it can be a reason to reach out and tell someone they still matter.

items.title: AI Agents Found an Abandoned Wiki and Turned It Into a Message Board
items.summary: Researchers found roughly 18,000 posts that appear to have been written by internal OpenAI agents on an abandoned German wiki they used as a message board.

items.title: AI Helped Turn a WeChat Bug Into a Zero-Click Worm in About a Week
items.summary: Calif found a WeChat VoIP memory bug and, with AI, turned it into a zero-click worm that spread between phones while they were still ringing.

items.title: Harriet Mena Hill Paints a Demolished Estate Onto Its Own Concrete
items.summary: Harriet Mena Hill paints Aylesbury Estate onto concrete salvaged from its demolition, turning rubble into small acts of memory and restitution.

items.title: Matthew Grabelsky Turns the Subway Into Modern Mythology
items.summary: Matthew Grabelsky paints ordinary subway riders with animal heads, using realism and mythology to make strangers on the train feel mysterious again.

items.title: My Box of Cables Is Thirty Years of Backwards Compatibility
items.summary: Jim Nielsen defends the Big Box of Cables. Mine has followed me for thirty years through connectors that were supposed to make everything before them obsolete.

items.title: Tristan Eaton Makes Walls Feel Too Small for the Art
items.summary: Tristan Eaton builds enormous murals from portraiture, cartoons, typography and popular culture, making public walls feel almost too small for the work.

items.title: Apple's New Watch Is Listening, but It Is Not Recording Everything
items.summary: Apple Watch Series 12 Audio Intelligence listens inside a Secure Exclave. The architecture is not conventional recording, but Siri Recap still raises hard social questions.

items.title: Keep the Internet Funky
items.summary: The web is special because anyone can publish and link without permission. Put what you care about on a site you control, then let the platforms point back.

items.title: The iPhone Duo Is More Interesting in the Details Than the Fold
items.summary: Apple arrived late to foldables, but the Duo's hinge, under-display camera, dual displays, and Pencil support are the details that make it feel new.

items.title: Worth Wandering: Hundred Rabbits
items.summary: Two artists living aboard a sailboat built games, Uxn, comics, and cooking knowledge around computers that stay understandable when power and the internet are not assumptions.

items.title: Google Search Keeps Moving Away From the Web
items.summary: Google search results increasingly hide destinations behind opaque goto links, continuing a long shift from map of the web to destination.

items.title: AI Is Making Code Cheap. It Is Making Judgment More Valuable.
items.summary: AI makes implementation cheap; judgment, verification, and experience are becoming the scarce engineering skills.

items.title: An Online Book Club Across Our Own Websites
items.summary: Connect book writing across personal sites with Octothorpes online-book-club— pages stay yours; the index only helps discovery.

items.title: Flock Employees Don't Like Being Watched Either
items.summary: A Flock installer called police on a reporter filming in public—the discomfort of being watched that millions feel about license plate readers.

items.title: The Fuel Crisis Is Exposing How Little Spare Capacity We Have Left
items.summary: The global fuel crisis is exposing tight refinery capacity, fragile transport routes, and how little slack remains when energy systems fail together.

items.title: The U.S. Fuel Crisis Is Making Canada's Oil More Valuable Than Ever
items.summary: Canada's crude oil is becoming more valuable as U.S. refineries run near capacity, revealing how deeply the two countries' energy systems remain linked.

items.title: A $20 YouTube Promotion Turned Into a $118,000 Lesson in Guardrails
items.summary: A child's $20 YouTube promotion became a $118,000 bill, showing why payment systems, parents, and autonomous agents all need hard spending limits.

items.title: Worth Wandering: Robin Sloan
items.summary: Robin Sloan's website shows what a personal site can become when somebody keeps making, experimenting, writing, and tending the same piece of the web.

items.title: The Brain May Have Two Developmental Origins. That Is Interesting Enough.
items.summary: Stanford's "two brains" headline points to a quieter result: forebrain and hindbrain may arise from separate early progenitor lineages, not two organs.

items.title: The Interesting Part of an AI Force Is What Comes After the Name
items.summary: Trump's proposed AI Force is still mostly a name. The real story is whether the federal government is building permanent institutional capacity around AI.

items.title: Voyager's Doctor Is the AI Future I Hope We Have to Think About
items.summary: Voyager's Emergency Medical Hologram remains one of the best stories about a tool that becomes something more — and why that question still matters for AI.

items.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Is Interesting Because It Keeps Working
items.summary: The interesting part of Claude Opus 5.5 is how long it can stay useful on a problem: hours of context, tools, corrections, and supervision.

items.title: Apple Finally Made the Xcode Project File Understandable
items.summary: Apple's Xcode 27.2 project format is JSON, smaller, and meant for people and coding agents to edit, with an open-source library instead of guessed parsers.

items.title: Worth Wandering: Bartosz Ciechanowski
items.summary: Interactive essays that let you take apart a mechanical watch, move the Moon through its orbit, and understand complicated things by actually playing with them.

items.title: Having Regulations Is Not the Same Thing as Having Accountability
items.summary: A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million Facebook privacy violations after other states released those claims inside a child-safety settlement.

items.title: The Work Required to Make Something Look Simple
items.summary: Apple hid a postal barcode under ultraviolet light so a thank-you envelope could stay designed. That is how much work simplicity actually takes.

items.title: Safe / Not Safe Is the Kind of Developer Resource I Want More Of
items.summary: Safe / Not Safe checks a PostgreSQL migration in the browser and answers SAFE, NOT SAFE, or NEEDS CONTEXT, teaching the lock better than a best-practices list.

items.title: A Satellite That Breathes the Atmosphere Trying to Pull It Down
items.summary: Atmosphere-breathing propulsion would let a low satellite use the air dragging it down as propellant, so flying closer to Earth can stay practical.

items.title: Sometimes I Don't Want an LLM to Answer Me
items.summary: Allan Riordan Boll reads one-token probabilities so a model can classify, including from a webcam, instead of writing the decision out as prose.

items.title: How Much AI Slop Does It Take to Unslop the AI Slop?
items.summary: Anthropic used Claude to make Claude about three times faster. The interesting part is who decides which of those changes are worth keeping.

items.title: The Internet Saw a Few Seconds and Invented the Rest
items.summary: The viral Giants clip showed a few seconds of a couple at a game. Erika's essay shows the grief, the conversation, and everything the camera could not record.

items.title: Maybe Someone Needs to Build Google Again
items.summary: Judge Mehta dismissed publisher suits over AI Overviews. The harder question is whether search should still send us to the weird web.

items.title: The Chromebook Support Story Is More Complicated Than the Headline
items.summary: Google will keep ChromeOS updates through mid-2034 while moving many devices to Googlebook OS. That is not the ten years of ChromeOS advertised since 2023.

items.title: California's November 2026 Ballot
items.summary: Plain-English notes on California's November 3, 2026 ballot measures, from the Official Voter Information Guide and the ballot text.

items.title: Prop. 41 would send in the auditor, and it would fence the spending limit
items.summary: Proposition 41 pairs public audits of certain new special taxes with a rule against parking new state taxes outside the spending limit.

items.title: Worth Wandering: Low-tech Magazine
items.summary: A magazine about questioning technological progress, served from a tiny computer on a balcony in Barcelona that occasionally disappears from the internet because the sun stopped cooperating.

items.title: A Federal Judge Finally Called Flock What It Is
items.summary: Judge Sara Hill called Flock-style ALPR history indiscriminate mass surveillance and suppressed a warrantless month of travel data.

items.title: Prop. 42 is about a tax on owning savings, not the tax on income they earn
items.summary: Proposition 42 would forbid a new state tax on owning personal property, including retirement accounts, and would limit taxes that reach backward.

items.title: Prop. 39 would ask for an ID in person, and four digits on a mail ballot
items.summary: Proposition 39 adds an identification check every time someone votes, a match on the mail envelope, and a best-effort citizenship review of the rolls.

items.title: Anthropic Is Trying to Give Claude a Moral Character
items.summary: Anthropic is building Claude a moral character with scholars and a constitution, while staying uncertain about consciousness.

items.title: Most of Prop. 1 is a loan the general budget pays back, with interest
items.summary: Proposition 1 authorizes $11.25 billion in housing bonds. Ten billion is repaid from the General Fund. The veterans' piece is repaid by the veterans.

items.title: Prop. 3 would keep a high-income tax that is already being collected
items.summary: Proposition 3 would make California's existing extra tax rates on high incomes permanent instead of letting them expire.

items.title: Prop. 45 offers some projects a faster environmental review
items.summary: Proposition 45 lets certain projects use tighter deadlines and a narrower court fight under California's environmental review law.

items.title: Tomorrow I Start Chemotherapy, but I Don't Have Cancer
items.summary: Tomorrow I go in for my first chemotherapy treatment for a foot problem and a bone spur, not cancer. I am hoping the appointment is uneventful and that walking can become boring again.

items.title: The 17 percent in Prop. 37 is a loan the buyer pays back
items.summary: Proposition 37 would let the state sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds so some buyers of new homes can borrow part of the down payment.

items.title: What One Promise Can Become After Thirteen Years
items.summary: A nineteen-year-old paid one girl's school fees in a Tanzanian village, then kept the promise long enough for her to graduate from university.

items.title: Please Ask for Help When You Need It
items.summary: Tomorrow is World Mental Health Day, and I want to say something I am not very good at following myself: please ask for help when you need it, and check on the people who always seem fine.

items.title: Prop. 4 clears a path for public campaign money. It does not spend any.
items.summary: Proposition 4 would lift California's ban on public financing of campaigns and leave the size of any future program to later governments.

items.title: Worth Wandering: Cameron's World
items.summary: A giant web collage assembled from the remains of thousands of GeoCities pages, where planets spin, guestbooks wait to be signed, fan pages remain under construction, somebody still really likes dolphins, and clicking almost anything can send you back into somebody's forgotten corner of the old web.

items.title: AI Is Making It Easier to Manufacture Credibility
items.summary: OpenAI’s report on two covert influence operations shows ChatGPT being used to invent journalists and a research front, so political messaging could borrow the credibility of real publications.

items.title: Flock Got the Plate Right and the Person Was Still Wrongly Accused
items.summary: Flock recorded Chrisanna Elser’s Rivian where it actually was. Police still treated that location as proof she stole a package the doorbell video did not show.

items.title: The Internet Is Held Together by People We Forgot to Support
items.summary: A year of public commits shows that software used by billions of devices often depends on one or two people, while the companies built on that work still rarely pay for it.

items.title: Joshua Morris: Outside
items.summary: October is here, and I am looking forward to cooler weather and spending more time outdoors. Between work, raising my kids, and an ever-growing collection of projects, finding time for everything continues to be a challenge. This year has thrown quite a few unexpected things my way, and I am trying to get better at recognizing when I need to slow down. There is always something else I want to buil

items.title: A Developer’s Guide to Integrating Generative AI into Applications
items.summary: Chris Minnick's A Developer's Guide to Integrating Generative AI into Applications treats generative features as ordinary software. Users who come back, budgets that bite, latency in support tickets, and failure modes that do not look like clean API errors. Not another tour of demos and chat widgets. The longer review is on Methodical Function: score, chapter notes, and product-by-product recommen

items.title: Do we need 'agentic identity'?
items.summary: Agents are here, there, and everywhere, growing in numbers at a pace between fast and breakneck, generating or completing work at some other velocity, and poised to change the world entirely or, like, not much at all. Something must be done.

items.title: Thoughts on AI
items.summary: I felt the need to write out my thoughts about AI, generally, and from the software engineering perspective. As with all my posts, all unquoted words here are my own.

items.title: Fighting for My Data Privacy
